summary: Specifies the Lower-Effort Per-Hop Behavior for Differentiated Services, which protects best-effort traffic from lower-effort traffic during congestion. It can also serve as a scavenger service class. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: The Lower-Effort per-hop behavior is a traffic class for data that does not matter much if it is delayed or lost. Packets marked for it are dropped before ordinary traffic when a network is busy, so they use only the capacity nobody else wants.

subtitle: A traffic class for data that should only use the network when nobody else wants it.

tldr.problem: Traffic such as backups, software updates and telemetry has no urgency, yet it competes with ordinary traffic when a link is busy. The earlier recommendation to mark it CS1 could even make it win over best-effort traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The Lower-Effort (LE) per-hop behavior gives marked packets lower precedence than the default behavior, so they are dropped first in congestion and may be starved. The RFC recommends the new DSCP 000001 for this class.
tldr.outcome: Because best-effort traffic keeps precedence, LE traffic cannot crowd it out. RFC 8622 obsoletes RFC 3662 and moves RFC 4594 and RFC 8325 from CS1 to the LE codepoint.

today: RFC 8622 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3662 and updates RFC 4594 and RFC 8325, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its recommended codepoint is the DSCP 000001.

sections.title: A Traffic Class That Yields to Others
sections.content:
This document defines a Differentiated Services (DS) per-hop behavior called the Lower-Effort Per-Hop Behavior (LE PHB). It is intended for traffic of sufficiently low urgency that all other traffic takes precedence over it in the consumption of network link bandwidth. Low urgency does not mean the traffic is unimportant; it means the traffic has a low priority for timely forwarding, in the way a network is the equivalent of a background priority for processes in an operating system. There may or may not be memory resources allocated for this type of traffic.

The LE PHB has two important properties. It should scavenge residual capacity, using only resources that no other traffic is demanding. And it must be preemptable by the default PHB, or by other elevated PHBs, when those need more resources. The effect of this traffic on all other network traffic is therefore strictly limited, which the document calls the "no harm" property.

This is distinct from Best-Effort (BE) traffic. The network makes no commitment to deliver LE packets, while BE traffic receives an implied good faith commitment of at least some available network resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Some traffic does not need to arrive quickly. This document defines a class for it. Packets in this class are dropped before ordinary packets when a link is busy, so they take only the capacity that would otherwise go unused.

sections.title: Which Traffic Fits the LE Behavior
sections.content:
The LE PHB is suitable for applications that would otherwise use BE delivery and that can tolerate strongly varying throughput, especially periods of very low throughput or even starvation, meaning long interruptions caused by significant or complete packet loss. An application sending an LE-marked flow therefore needs to be able to tolerate short or very long interruptions, and packets of the LE PHB can be excessively delayed or dropped whenever other traffic is present. Whether a lack of progress counts as a failure is application dependent.

Just like BE traffic, LE traffic should be congestion controlled, and transport protocols or applications should be able to detect and react to starvation. An appropriate reaction is to resume the transfer rather than abort it, using retry strategies such as exponential back-off with an upper bound. Where no LE-adapted transport is available, applications can use common transport protocols and re-establish failed connections.

The document lists example uses: traffic caused by web search engines while they gather information from web servers, software updates or dissemination of new operating system releases, error reports and telemetry data, backup traffic and non-time-critical synchronization, content distribution transfers between caches, preloading or prefetching objects from web sites, bulk mail, and multicast traffic from untrusted sources. The LE PHB should not be used for a customer's normal Internet traffic, and packets should not be downgraded to LE instead of being dropped, particularly when they are unauthorized traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Use this class for traffic that can wait: backups, software updates, telemetry, and bulk transfers. The sending application has to be prepared for the transfer to stall for a long time and then start again, so it should use congestion control and a retry policy that backs off.

sections.title: How Routers Treat LE Traffic
sections.content:
The LE PHB is defined in relation to the default PHB (BE). A packet forwarded with the LE PHB should have lower precedence than a packet forwarded with the default PHB, so in congestion LE-marked traffic should be dropped before any default PHB traffic. Ideally, LE packets would be forwarded only when no packet with any other PHB is awaiting transmission. That means LE traffic can be starved completely in the case of link resource contention, which may not always be what the network operator wants, so a scheduler used to implement the LE PHB may reflect that policy accordingly.

A straightforward implementation is a simple priority scheduler serving the default PHB queue with higher priority than the LE PHB queue. Alternative implementations may use scheduling algorithms that assign a very small weight to the LE class, although that can sometimes give LE packets better service than BE packets when the BE share is fully used and the LE share is not.

If a dedicated LE queue is not available, an active queue management mechanism within a common BE and LE queue can also be used, dropping all arriving LE packets as soon as certain queue length or sojourn time thresholds are exceeded.

Because congestion control is also useful within the LE class, Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) should be used for LE packets too. An LE implementation should also apply Congestion Experienced (CE) marking for ECN-Capable Transport (ECT) marked packets, and transport protocols used for LE should support and employ ECN.
sections.plainLanguage: A router puts LE packets in their own queue and serves that queue only when the ordinary queue is empty. When both queues are full, LE packets are the ones dropped. Because LE packets may wait a long time, routers can also mark them as congestion experienced, so the sender slows down instead of losing data.

sections.title: Marking LE Traffic
sections.content:
If possible, packets should be pre-marked in DS-aware end systems by the applications, because the application knows the precedence its own packets deserve. There is no incentive for DS domains to distrust this initial marking, because letting LE traffic enter a DS domain causes no harm, so policing such as limiting the rate of LE traffic is not necessary at the DS boundary.

As with most other PHBs, an initial classification and marking can also be performed at the first DS boundary node according to the domain's own policies, for example as a protection measure against untrusted sources. However, non-LE traffic, such as BE traffic, should not be re-marked to LE. Re-marking traffic from another PHB downgrades it, which changes the way the network treats that traffic, and it is important not to violate the operational objectives of the original PHB.
sections.plainLanguage: The application that sends the data should mark it, because it knows how urgent the data is. A router at the edge of the network may also mark it. What a router should not do is take ordinary traffic and downgrade it to this class, because that traffic was promised better service.

sections.title: The Recommended DSCP
sections.content:
The recommended codepoint for the LE PHB is '000001'. Earlier specifications, such as RFC 4594, recommended Class Selector 1 (CS1) as the codepoint. That is problematic, because it may cause a priority inversion in Diffserv domains that treat CS1 as originally proposed in RFC 2474, resulting in LE packets being forwarded with higher precedence than BE packets. Existing implementations should transition to the unambiguous LE codepoint '000001' whenever possible.

This particular codepoint was chosen because of measurements on the currently observable DSCP re-marking behavior in the Internet. Since some network domains set the former IP Precedence bits to zero, it is possible that some other standardized DSCPs would get mapped to the LE PHB DSCP if it were taken from the DSCP Standards Action Pool 1 (xxxxx0).

The document assigns the DSCP '000001' from the Differentiated Services Field Codepoints registry, in the "DSCP Pool 3 Codepoints" space xxxx01, Standards Action. IANA has updated that registry with the name LE, the binary value 000001, the decimal value 1, and a reference to RFC 8622.
sections.plainLanguage: The class is marked with the six-bit code 000001 in the DSCP field of the IP header. The older code for this job, CS1, was a bad choice, because some networks treat CS1 as more important than ordinary traffic, which would put this low-priority class ahead of the traffic it is supposed to yield to.

sections.title: Deploying LE Support
sections.content:
To support LE, a DS node typically needs only three things: a behavior aggregate classifier that classifies packets according to the LE DSCP, a dedicated LE queue, and a suitable scheduling discipline such as simple priority queueing. Alternatively, implementations can use active queue management instead of a dedicated queue, for example dropping all arriving LE packets when certain queue length or sojourn time thresholds are exceeded.

Deployment is eased by three properties. LE causes no harm to other traffic, because it has the lowest forwarding priority and does not consume resources from other PHBs, so providers can trust LE markings from end systems without policing or re-marking. The PHB has no parameters to set and no traffic profiles to configure, because LE traffic requires no admission or policing. And it needs no traffic-conditioning mechanisms: no meters, droppers or shapers.

Operators of DS domains that cannot or do not want to implement the LE PHB, for example because no separate LE queue is available, should not drop packets marked with the LE DSCP. They should map those packets to the default PHB and should preserve the LE DSCP marking. Such operators should be aware that forwarding LE traffic with the default PHB violates the no harm property of LE.

For multicast, the considerations of RFC 3754 apply, with the added complication that packet replication inside routers can create contention before a packet reaches an output port. A replication mechanism for LE-marked packets should check the state of the output links, because replicating a packet to a link whose LE queue is full wastes internal resources. Conditional internal replication would avoid this, but it is probably not widely implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that wants to support this class needs a classifier, a separate queue for the class, and a way to serve that queue last. Networks that do not implement it should still carry the marked packets rather than drop them, and should keep the marking so that later networks can still treat them correctly.

sections.title: Re-marking and the Updates to Other RFCs
sections.content:
DSCP bleaching, which means setting the DSCP to '000000' for the default PHB, is not recommended for this PHB. It can have effects that contradict the original intent of protecting BE traffic from LE traffic. A DS domain that does not support the LE PHB should treat LE-marked packets with the default PHB by mapping the LE DSCP to the default PHB, but should do so without re-marking to DSCP '000000', because domains traversed later may then still have the opportunity to treat the packets according to the LE PHB.

Operators who forward LE traffic within the BE aggregate should be aware of the implications, which are induced congestion and quality-of-service degradation of the original BE traffic. In that case the no harm property is no longer fulfilled, and traffic policing of the LE aggregate may be used to limit the impact. Applications that want to keep the lower precedence even in that case should additionally use a lower-than-BE transport protocol such as LEDBAT.

A DS domain that still uses DSCP CS1 for marking LE traffic, including the Low-Priority Data class of RFC 4594, should re-mark traffic to the LE DSCP '000001' at the egress to the next DS domain, because a CS1-marked packet may be re-marked to the default DSCP if the next domain applies Diffserv-Interconnection.

The document also updates two other specifications. In RFC 4594, every occurrence of the CS1 DSCP is replaced by the LE DSCP: the Low-Priority Data entry of Figure 3 changes from CS1 with value 001000 to LE with value 000001, the matching entry in Figure 4 changes from RFC3662 to RFC 8622, the note below Figure 3 is extended, and Section 4.10 now says that the recommended DSCP marking is LE, which replaces the prior recommendation for CS1. A further passage in Section 2.3 of RFC 4594, which recommended re-marking to 000xx1 on ingress in segments that use IP precedence marking, is removed, because the LE DSCP makes such re-marking unnecessary. In RFC 8325, Section 4.2.10 is updated to say that RFC 3662 recommends that Low-Priority Data be marked CS1 while RFC 4594, as updated by RFC 8622, recommends that it be marked LE, and the recommendation to map Low-Priority Data traffic marked with LE DSCP or legacy CS1 DSCP to UP 1 replaces the older CS1-only wording.
sections.plainLanguage: A network that carries this class as ordinary traffic must not erase the marking, because a later network would then have no way to treat the packets correctly. Networks that still use the old CS1 code should change it to the new LE code at the edge of their domain, and the RFC fixes the wording in the two earlier specifications that still recommended CS1.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
There are no specific security exposures for this PHB. Because it defines a new class that has a low forwarding priority, re-marking other traffic as LE traffic may lead to quality-of-service degradation of that traffic. An attacker able to modify the DSCP of a packet to LE may therefore carry out a downgrade attack. The general security considerations of RFC 2474 and RFC 2475 apply.

With respect to privacy, an attacker could use the DSCP to infer that transferred content, even if encrypted, is considered low priority or low urgency by a user, if the DSCP was set at the user's request. That information is useful only if it can be correlated with metadata such as the user's IP address or with other flows that reveal the user's identity. It might also help an observer interested in learning about a user's behavior, since LE-marked background traffic such as software downloads or telemetry may be less interesting than general web traffic, which lets the observer focus on traffic that may be more interesting.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no new attack surface here, but a network attacker can rewrite the marking and push another user's traffic down to this low class, which degrades that traffic. The marking also says something about the sender's priorities, though the leak is small on its own.

items.title: Scavenges residual capacity
items.text: Uses only the link capacity that no other traffic is demanding.

items.title: Preemptable by the default PHB
items.text: Dropped before ordinary traffic when the link is congested, and may be starved.

items.title: No harm to other traffic
items.text: The effect on all other traffic in the network is strictly limited.
